title: Eastern Air Lines, Inc. v. Gulf Oil Corp.
lead: When oil-market changes made a long-term fuel price formula less favorable to Gulf Oil, Gulf threatened to stop supplying Eastern Air Lines. After trial, the district court held the requirements contract enforceable, rejected Gulf’s impracticability defenses, and permanently ordered continued supply at the agreed prices.

actors.name: Eastern Air Lines
actors.role: Airline buying its fuel requirements at specified locations.

actors.name: Gulf Oil Corporation
actors.role: Supplier that drafted the long-term contract and selected the price index.

actors.name: Judge James Lawrence King
actors.role: District judge who made the trial findings and entered permanent relief.

proceedings: Eastern sought preliminary and permanent mandatory relief. An agreed preliminary injunction maintained performance during litigation; after trial the court made it permanent. Deferred price counterclaim became moot by the parties’ agreement.
limits: The opinion is a single district-court decision applying then-existing Florida Uniform Commercial Code provisions and energy controls. It does not hold that all requirement changes are permissible or that a profitable corporation can never prove impracticability.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The parties choose a requirements bargain and a specific index
sections.cue: Both sides obtain advantages from a long-term arrangement.
paragraphs: Eastern Air Lines and Gulf Oil Corporation had traded aviation fuel for decades. Gulf began arm’s-length negotiations more than a year before existing agreements expired. On June 27, 1972, they signed Gulf’s standard-form contract, consolidating and extending supply through January 31, 1977 at specified cities. Gulf obtained a long-term market for new refinery capacity; Eastern received immediate price savings. Eastern had to buy its fuel requirements at the covered locations from Gulf, and Gulf had to supply reasonable good-faith demands.

Expecting crude prices to rise, the parties replaced an escalator that passed through only half of increases with one intended to transmit crude-cost changes proportionately. They selected the average posted price for West Texas sour crude of a specified gravity, quoted by Gulf, Shell, and Pan American in Platts Oilgram’s crude supplement. Prices were already regulated. Eastern’s jet-fuel payments rose from roughly eleven to fifteen cents per gallon as that indicator increased.

sections.title: The energy crisis separates the index from other crude costs
sections.cue: A declaration of nonperformance precedes the later supply ultimatum.
paragraphs: The 1973 crisis combined war, an Arab oil embargo, sharp foreign crude-price increases, and domestic two-tier controls. Under the court’s account, output at a well’s May 1972 level was controlled old oil; added output was new oil, accompanied by release of a matching amount of old oil from controls. A well rising from 100 to 150 barrels therefore produced fifty controlled and one hundred uncontrolled barrels. Platts continued reporting the specified old-oil postings but not premiums for new and released oil. The contract index consequently did not track every increase in Gulf’s crude purchases. Eastern paid according to the index.

The court ultimately identified Gulf’s December 31, 1973 declaration that the contract was no longer effective as a breach. By March 8, 1974 Gulf demanded a price increase and threatened to stop supplying Eastern within fifteen days. Eastern sued for mandatory preliminary and permanent relief. An agreed March 20 injunction required supply and payment according to the contract.

Gulf challenged mutuality and definiteness, accused Eastern of manipulating requirements, and asserted commercial impracticability under Florida’s Uniform Commercial Code sections 2-614 and 2-615. Eastern’s other counts alleging tort, antitrust, and federal-energy violations were struck on Gulf’s motion. Gulf’s counterclaim seeking a judicially determined fuel price was deferred by agreement and would become moot if Eastern prevailed on its contract claim.

sections.title: The requirements obligation is definite and was performed in good faith
sections.cue: Established tankering practices do not establish manipulation.
paragraphs: Judge James Lawrence King found a valid requirements contract under section 2-306. Actual good-faith business requirements measured quantity, constrained by unreasonable disproportionality to stated estimates or comparable prior demands. Eastern could not demand any amount at whim. Long dealing confirmed exclusivity at covered stations and Gulf’s duty to meet reasonable requirements. Estimates existed for some locations and were exchanged more often under petroleum allocations.

Eastern’s fuel freighting, also called tankering, did not breach the bargain. Airlines can take extra fuel at cheaper stations and less at later expensive ones within operational limits. Requirements also change with schedules, weather, aircraft, passenger loads, turnaround time, taxes, and pilots’ judgment. Gulf knew these practices and had accepted substantial fluctuations for decades, including particular large increases without objection. The practices were commercially established and part of these parties’ performance and dealing. Merchant good faith included honesty and reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing.

The court preserved section 2-306’s protection against unreasonable demands and did not decide hypothetical extremes. On the actual record, Gulf was objecting after the dispute arose to previously accepted features of the trade. Eastern had continued performing.

sections.title: The agreed index still operates and Gulf does not prove its claimed hardship
sections.cue: Internal accounting figures do not establish this contract’s cost.
paragraphs: Gulf argued both that controls defeated the escalator’s purpose and that higher crude prices made performance commercially impracticable. The judge addressed section 2-615 on the merits despite Eastern’s notice objection because Gulf had identified the defense in its summer 1974 opposition memorandum and later answer.

The specified quotations remained available and calculable. Clear contract language selected those postings, not an unspecified measure of every Gulf input cost. They were controlled when selected and remained so; Gulf still used old-oil prices in intercompany agreements, and substantial domestic production remained old oil. The publication-suspension clause did not apply because Platts kept publishing the quotations and Gulf had not followed its notice-and-substitution procedure.

Gulf also failed to prove actual hardship in supplying Eastern. Its witnesses could not identify the production cost of a gallon of jet fuel, whether these sales lost money, or how that changed over time. Average crude-cost figures included transfer prices and profits allocated among subsidiaries. Foreign-crude margins had risen substantially; domestic recorded production cost was far below the transfer-price figure used for average refining cost. The evidence did not reveal all internal margins.

Gulf could maximize profits and structure its business, but those choices did not prove legal hardship or require preservation of internal profits as external expenses. Record company profits reinforced the conclusion without replacing missing contract-cost evidence. The ruling did not make overall profitability a categorical bar to impracticability.

sections.title: Risk allocation supplies an independent reason to enforce the bargain
sections.cue: A price disappointment is not failure of the means of payment.
paragraphs: Even if serious hardship had been established, the court considered Middle Eastern volatility, supply interruption, host-government control, expected crude increases, and changing domestic controls sufficiently foreseeable business risks for Gulf to address. Gulf executives were deeply engaged in federal petroleum-policy discussions. Eastern’s negotiator anticipated shortages and regulatory limits on price increases. Gulf drafted the contract and selected the domestic postings; the judge held Gulf to that selection.

Section 2-614(2) did not provide another escape. It addresses regulatory failure of an agreed means or manner of payment, such as prohibition of a specified monetary medium. Nothing here prevented the agreed payment mechanism. The complaint concerned the amount of the contractual price.

sections.title: The court orders continued supply for the contract term
sections.cue: The existing preliminary arrangement becomes permanent.
paragraphs: Gulf stipulated that it could perform, and the preliminary arrangement had worked for more than a year. Gulf supplied approximately one hundred million gallons annually, about ten percent of Eastern’s needs. Abrupt cessation threatened chaos and irreparable injury. Under section 2-716’s more liberal specific-performance standard, the judge regarded continued supply at contract prices as the natural relief.

The final findings established a valid agreement, Eastern’s continued performance, Gulf’s December 31 breach, and failure of Gulf’s formation and impracticability defenses. The mandatory preliminary injunction became permanent. Under counsel’s agreement, Gulf’s deferred price counterclaim became moot; the court did not award a judicially adjusted price. This was one district judge’s findings and conclusions, without an appellate vote or separate opinion.
